# Everest, North Dakota

**Everest** is an unincorporated community in Everest Township, Cass County, North Dakota, United States. Located south of Casselton, it was platted in 1881 and served as a notable railroad hub and agricultural center in the late 19th century. The community experienced substantial prosperity during its early years but declined following the removal of a major rail line and a series of destructive fires. As of 2020, Everest Township had a population of 99, though Everest itself has been removed from official county maps.

# History

### Founding and early development

Everest was platted in 1881 during the period of intensive railroad development and settlement expansion across Dakota Territory. The post office was established on May 24, 1882, with Carl Knuppel serving as the first postmaster. The community benefited from its strategic location at the junction of two major rail lines: the Great Northern Railway and the Northern Pacific Railway, making it an important shipping point for agricultural products from the surrounding region.

During the late 1880s and 1890s, Everest became a prosperous community with a diverse economy. At its height, the town boasted over 200 residents and included a railroad depot, post office, two hotels, a school, a church, two general stores, two saloons, a butcher shop, a blacksmith shop, a lumber yard, and four grain elevators, along with various other businesses including a harness maker.

### The Langer family connection

Everest gained prominence in North Dakota history as the birthplace of William Langer, who would become the 17th and later 21st governor of North Dakota and a United States senator. Born on September 30, 1886, near Everest to German-American parents Frank and Mary (Weber) Langer, William Langer spent his early childhood in the community before eventually relocating to pursue his political career. Frank Langer, William's father, was a member of the first North Dakota state legislature, making the Langer family prominent residents of the Everest area during the late 1800s. Joseph Langer, William's uncle, also became a prominent member of the community.

### Economic importance and decline

The community's fortunes changed following significant structural changes in regional railroad infrastructure. Around 1896, the westernmost of the two rail lines—which had connected the Great Northern Railway and the Northern Pacific Railway—was removed when it was acquired by the Great Northern Railway. This loss of rail competition and connectivity substantially reduced Everest's economic importance.

Compounding the effects of railroad decline, a series of disastrous fires devastated the community's commercial infrastructure. The combination of these fires and the closure of the post office in 1908 accelerated Everest's decline. By 1960, most of the community's establishments had permanently closed, leaving Everest with a population of just 10 residents. The community has since been removed from official county maps.

# Notable residents

Beyond the Langer family, Everest was home to several individuals who achieved prominence in North Dakota. James Trammell, Edward Meilicke, Edward Redmon, Edward Weber, Edward Arnold, William MacFadden, and August Hilke each served as Everest Township or Cass County officials.

**Herbert Nilles**, a resident of the Everest area, was elected to the presidency of the North Dakota State Bar. **Morgan Ford**, born in Wheatland, North Dakota, was appointed as a judge of the United States Customs Court (later known as the Court of International Trade) by President Harry S. Truman in 1949. Although Ford was born in Wheatland, his family connections to the Everest area were significant enough that he is noted among the community's prominent figures.

# Geography

Everest is located 20 miles (32 km) from Fargo, the county seat of Cass County, and 2 miles (3.2 km) south of Casselton. The community lies at the junction of North Dakota Highway 18 and 155th Avenue SE, in close proximity to the Casselton Robert Miller Regional Airport.

Everest Township, which contains the unincorporated community, has a total area of 35.08 square miles (90.9 km²). As of the 2020 census, the township had a population of 99, and as of 2023, there were an estimated 26 households in the township.

**William** "**Wild Bill**" **Langer** (September 30, 1886 – November 8, 1959) was an American lawyer and politician who served as the 17th [governor of North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_North_Dakota "Governor of North Dakota") from 1932 to 1934 and the 21st governor from 1937 to 1939. His governorship was demarcated by a scandal that forced him out of office and into multiple trials.

Langer was elected to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") in 1940, serving until he died in office in 1959. As a senator, he strongly opposed American military involvement in world affairs, being derided by his opponents as an isolationist.

Early life, education and early career
--------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_Langer&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life, education and early career")\]

Langer was born on September 30, 1886, near [Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota "Everest, North Dakota"), [Dakota Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_Territory "Dakota Territory"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-1) to [German-Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-American "German-American") Frank and Mary (Weber) Langer. His [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") father, Frank Langer, was a member of the first legislature of the state of North Dakota. William, who spoke [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") fluently,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-2) was valedictorian of Casselton High School upon graduation in 1904. He obtained a bachelor of laws from the [University of North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Dakota "University of North Dakota") in [Grand Forks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Forks,_North_Dakota "Grand Forks, North Dakota"), but was too young upon graduation to practice law. He therefore continued his undergraduate education at [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_College_of_Columbia_University "Columbia College of Columbia University"), where he graduated at the top of his class in 1910. Although he was offered a position at a prominent New York law firm, he elected to return to North Dakota, where he practiced law in [Mandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandan,_North_Dakota "Mandan, North Dakota") before starting his career in politics.

Langer married Lydia Cady, the daughter of New York architect [J. Cleaveland Cady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Cleaveland_Cady "J. Cleaveland Cady"), in 1918,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-3) and had four daughters, Emma, Lydia, Mary, and Cornelia (who became a wife of abstract painter [Kenneth Noland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Noland "Kenneth Noland")).

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Portrait_of_William_Langer%2C_circa_1919.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_William_Langer%2C_circa_1919.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_William_Langer,_circa_1919.jpg)

Langer as North Dakota Attorney General c. 1919

In 1914, Langer was appointed state's attorney of [Morton County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_County,_North_Dakota "Morton County, North Dakota") and was one of a few non-farmers on the [Nonpartisan League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonpartisan_League "Nonpartisan League") (NPL) [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Republican_Party "North Dakota Republican Party") 1916 state ticket. He was elected state attorney general as the newly formed NPL party swept to victory in the 1916 election, but soon clashed with the party's founder and mercurial leader [Arthur C. Townley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_C._Townley "Arthur C. Townley"). By 1920, Langer was publicly accusing Townley of [Bolshevism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolshevism "Bolshevism"), and failed in a primary campaign to replace the incumbent NPL governor [Lynn Frazier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Frazier "Lynn Frazier") as the party's gubernatorial candidate. Langer's break with the NPL leadership was a reflection of the infighting that limited the party's eventual influence on North Dakota politics.

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Governor_William_Langer.jpg/250px-Governor_William_Langer.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Governor_William_Langer.jpg)

Langer as governor c. 1932–1939

Langer eventually mended his rift with the NPL and was elected governor of North Dakota in 1932. As governor, Langer in 1933 required all state employees to donate part of their annual salaries to the NPL and to the _Leader,_ a weekly newspaper owned by high-ranking officials in his administration. Collecting this money was not prohibited by state law and was a common, traditional practice. But when donations were made by highway department employees, who were paid through federal relief programs, the U.S. Attorney for North Dakota, [P. W. Lanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=P._W._Lanier&action=edit&redlink=1 "P. W. Lanier (page does not exist)"), charged that the donations constituted a conspiracy to defraud the federal government. Brought to trial in 1934, Langer and five co-conspirators were convicted. The trial was presided over by Judge [Andrew Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Miller_/(North_Dakota_judge/) "Andrew Miller (North Dakota judge)") and prosecuted by Lanier, two of Langer's strongest political opponents in the state.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-Vogel_2004-4)

The first trial was littered with procedural errors that made it invalid on appeal, including improper and rigged jury selection (the jurors were alleged to have had personal bias against Langer and been hand-picked by Lanier) and heavily biased jury instructions.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-Vogel_2004-4)

Because of the felony conviction, the [North Dakota Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Supreme_Court "North Dakota Supreme Court") on September 19, 1934, ordered Langer removed from office and declared Lieutenant Governor [Ole H. Olson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ole_H._Olson "Ole H. Olson") the legitimate governor.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-5) Langer signed a Declaration of Independence of North Dakota, declared martial law in Bismarck, and barricaded himself in the [governor's mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Former_North_Dakota_Executive_Mansion "Former North Dakota Executive Mansion").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-6) He eventually relented when his own officers refused to recognize his authority, and Olson served the remainder of Langer's term as governor.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-7)

In 1935, the convictions were overturned on appeal.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-8) The case against Langer was retried twice in 1935. Miller, following a recusal motion by Langer, refused to step down as judge in the first retrial, which resulted in a hung jury. Between the second and third trials, Lanier filed charges against Langer for committing perjury in his recusal motion against Miller. This trial, unprecedented on perjury in an affidavit requesting a recusal, resulted in a [directed verdict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_verdict "Directed verdict") to acquit Langer. The second retrial of the original charges, presided over by a judge other than Miller, resulted in Langer's acquittal.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-Vogel_2004-4)

Throughout the trials, Langer maintained that he was innocent and the victim of a political vendetta by Miller and Lanier. He was [reelected governor in 1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_North_Dakota_gubernatorial_election "1936 North Dakota gubernatorial election"). Historian Lawrence Larsen has called Langer "a master of political theater".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-9)

Langer's wife, Lydia, ran for governor in [1934](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1934_North_Dakota_gubernatorial_election "1934 North Dakota gubernatorial election") but lost to Democratic candidate [Thomas H. Moodie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_H._Moodie "Thomas H. Moodie").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-und.edu-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-11)

In 1938, Langer [ran for the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_United_States_Senate_election_in_North_Dakota "1938 United States Senate election in North Dakota") as an independent, and received 42% of the vote, losing to Republican [Gerald Nye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Nye "Gerald Nye").

The 1940 Senate election was another very dramatic one. Langer defeated incumbent Lynn Frazier in the Republican primary, and then faced both the Democratic candidate, [Charles Joseph Vogel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Joseph_Vogel "Charles Joseph Vogel"), and Republican/NPL Congressman [William Lemke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lemke "William Lemke"), who declined to run for reelection to Congress in order to run for the Senate as an independent. Langer won the election with 38% of the vote.

Because of the trials mentioned above, Langer's qualifications were questioned under Article 1, Section 5 of the Constitution, which declares the U.S. Senate the ultimate judge of its members' elections, qualifications, and returns. The Senate seated Langer conditionally and began an investigation into his trials. The [Committee on Privileges and Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Privileges_and_Elections "United States Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections") found Langer guilty of "[moral turpitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_turpitude "Moral turpitude")" and unqualified to be a U.S. senator. The full Senate reversed the committee and voted to seat Langer.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-Vogel_2004-4) The vote to expel Langer failed, then needing 64 votes to reach the two-third majority to pass.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-12)

Biographer Glenn H. Smith calls Langer's Senate career "A Study in Isolationism, 1940–1959" and emphasizes his close ties with German American and Scandinavian American voters who bitterly remembered the First World War in the Dakotas and deeply distrusted Britain and the United Nations.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-13) Like Senator [Henrik Shipstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Shipstead "Henrik Shipstead") of Minnesota, Langer championed [non-interventionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-interventionism "Non-interventionism")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-14) and supported minimizing America's involvement in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). At home, he concentrated on making life easier for North Dakotan farmers by raising wheat prices and granting government relief. He was also adamant about implementing affordable healthcare for everyone. As a senator, he served on the Post Office, Civil Service and Indian Affairs committees. He and Shipstead were the only senators to vote against the [United Nations Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Charter "United Nations Charter") in 1945.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-und.edu-10) He was also one of seven senators to oppose full U.S. entry into the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-15)

After African-American organizations asked Langer to propose a bill for the federal government to pay for the repatriation of African-Americans to the African continent, he did so.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-brendagayleplummer-16) The bill, S. 1800, failed to pass.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-brendagayleplummer-16) Langer was a Zionist who supported the establishment of [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"). During World War II, he had also supported American action to rescue Jewish refugees.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-17)

In September 1950, Langer filibustered to prevent the override of President [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman")'s veto of the [McCarran Internal Security Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarran_Internal_Security_Act "McCarran Internal Security Act") for five hours before collapsing.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-18)

In 1951, Langer lobbied [John J. McCloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_J._McCloy "John J. McCloy"), the U.S. High Commissioner for Germany, to grant a reprieve to [Martin Sandberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Sandberger "Martin Sandberger"), a high-ranking SS official who had been convicted of crimes against humanity and war crimes for his role in the mass murder of Jews and others in Estonia during the [Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust "Holocaust").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-Smelser_55-19) Although sentenced to die by the tribunal of the [Einsatzgruppen trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einsatzgruppen_trial "Einsatzgruppen trial"), in no small part due to Langer's lobbying,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-Smelser_55-19) Sandberger's sentence was commuted and he served only 13 years in custody. He died in 2010, at the age of 98.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-FreiGolb-20)

After the [Nonpartisan League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonpartisan_League "Nonpartisan League") merged with the state Democratic party, Langer remained on the Republican ticket in the 1958 Senate elections and won without making a single campaign appearance in the state. He voted for the [Civil Rights Act of 1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1957 "Civil Rights Act of 1957").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-21) Langer died in Washington, D.C., on November 8, 1959. He was the last U.S. senator to [lie in state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_in_state "Lie in state") in the Senate Chamber until [Robert Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Byrd "Robert Byrd") of [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia") in 2010.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer#cite_note-22)

*   1914–1916: [State's Attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State%27s_Attorney "State's Attorney") for [Morton County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morton_County,_North_Dakota "Morton County, North Dakota")
*   1916–1920: [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General "Attorney General") of North Dakota
*   1933–1934: Governor of North Dakota (removed from office)
*   1937–1939: Governor of North Dakota
*   1941–1959: [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")

*   [_The Famine in Germany._](https://archive.org/details/46LangerThefamineingermany) Washington, DC: US Government Printing Office, 1946.

**Everest Township** is a [township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_township "Civil township") in [Cass County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Cass County, North Dakota"), [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota"), United States. The population was 99 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").

The [unincorporated community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unincorporated_area "Unincorporated area") of [Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota "Everest, North Dakota") is located in Everest Township.

Geography
---------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Everest_Township,_North_Dakota&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geography")\]

Everest Township has a total area of 35.08 square miles (90.9 km2), all land.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest_Township,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CenPopGazetteer2020-3)

ii 

# 358714 PREFACE 

The purpose of this research was to record the early life and political career of one of North Dakota's outstand ing political figures, the late William Langer. Due to the magnitude of Langer's endeavors, the study was limited to the high points of his career through his election to state office as North Dakota Attorney General in 1916. Although the work covers only the beginning of his long public service, it demonstrates the forcefulness, ability, and competence that eventually made William Langer the most popular political leader in North Dakota history. 

The writer is indebted to Dr. D. Jerome Tweton for his valuable criticism and guidance in the preparation of this study. Special acknowledgement is also due Dr. Elwyn B. Robinson for his invaluable assistance and Dr. Henry J. Tomasek for his helpful suggestions. Also the writer wishes to thank the members of the Langer family for their valuable information on their father and brother. The writer is also grateful to all who aided in the work, especially Daniel Rylance, Archivist at Chester Fritz Library, University of North Dakota, for his helpful archival guidance, and Mrs. William Leiferman for her assistance in typing. And last, but never least, the author's wife whose many hours of assist ance made this work possible.

iv ABSTRACT 

The purpose of this research was to record the early life and political career of the former Attorney General, Governor, and Senator from North Dakota, William Langer. Due to the magnitude of his career, the study was focused on his youth, his education, his first political campaign and election as Morton County States Attorney, his work as States Attorney, and his campaign and election as Attorney General of North Dakota in 1916. 

The procedure involved a detailed study of the first thirty years of Langer's life. This included inter views with three of his sisters, one of his daughters, and the utilization of other contemporary sources. His educational career at the University of North Dakota and at Columbia University, New York, was analysed through the Langer Papers, published materials, and school newspapers and records. His early political career as States Attorney (1915-1916) and his rise to attorney general were revealed through the Langer Papers, newspapers, and various secondary sources. 

In conclusion, the study reveals Langer as an am bitious, energetic, and determined young man with an intense desire to attain his goals. Combining his desire with ability, political skill, and diligence, Langer quickly achieved an impressive record and rose to political prominence in North Dakota. 

vCHAPTER I

THE FORMATIVE YEARS 

The morning of September 30, 1886, brought great joy to the Frank J. Langer farm hone near the small village of Everest five miles southwest of present-day Casselton, 

North Dakota. After four girls the birth of a boy, William Langer, fulfilled the hopes of the family for a brother and son.1 

The Langer name went far back into the history of the European countries of Germany and Austria. William Langer* *s paternal grandfather, Franz Langer, was born in one of the German states^ and emigrated to the United States in 1852. After a sailing-ship voyage of ninety days he arrived with his wife, Rosa Miller Langer, and their two sons, Joseph 

Interview with Mrs. Hattie McGurren (one of William Langer's sisters), St. Vincent's Home, Bismarck, North Dakota, March 2, 1967; Current Biography: Who's News and Why, 1952 (New York: H. H. Wilson and Co., 1953), p. 326. 

*

^Franz Langer's exact birthplace was not located. However, in a letter from Governor William Langer to Mr. Clay Langer, September 9, 1937, Langer Papers, Box Sixty-nine, File Folder Five, Personal File, September 12-23, 1937, Langer answered the man's inquiry ioout the birthplace of his grand father by stating: "My grandfather came from a little place near Vienna, Austria, in 1852." Whether or not he was born there was not stated. 

12

and Frank, in New York City with only four dollars in his pocket and no knowledge of the English language.3* *

Nonetheless, by "sheer determination" he was able to 

make his way to Watertown, Wisconsin,4 and then in 1861 to 

the fanning area near Plainview, Minnesota, where he settled 

down to the hard work of homesteading. In the following 

years he developed a valuable and productive farm. Meanwhile 

his sons matured and entered farming after receiving their 

early education in the Plainview public schools.3 

In 1877 the Franz Langers retired and left Plainview 

to live with their son, Joseph, who had settled near the 

town of Casselton. Their other son, Frank, made a trip to the area in the same year to obtain land. During his first 

trip he found that "the wind blew so strong it blew the hair 

off a dog's back." Two years later he moved his family to the land he had purchased southwest of Casselton, but nearer the smaller settlement of Everest. With great industry and 

good management he improved his property and added to it 

3Lewis F. Crawford, History of North Dakota (Chicago: 

The American Historical Society, Inc., 1931) , II, 412; Fargo 

Forum, February 7, 1917, April 11, 1936, and September 4, 

1938. Frank Langer's birthdate was August 22, 1849, and 

Joseph Langer's was January 22, 1852. 

^Casselton Reporter, April 10, 1935; Fargo Forum, 

April 11, 1936. 

^Crawford, History of North Dakota, II, 412. 3

while he became one of the most active men in the area.^ 

Frank Langer's wife, the former Mary Weber, was born 

into an aristocratic family on March 15, 1856, at Sandskon (sometimes given as Landsknon), Austria. When she was ayoung girl her family came to America and located at Owatonna, Minnesota, where she met her future husband. On December 7, 

1874, they were married at Wabasha, Minnesota, and five years later she and their first child, Hattie, moved with 

him to their new farm in Dakota Territory. During the follow 

ing years the family grew with the addition of three more 

girls and three boys. However, one of the boys, Arthur, died at the age of three months.6 7

In.these pioneering days Mrs. Langer became not only 

an inspiration to her husband but also a helping hand to others. She never forgot her homeland and often helped troubled families from Austria settle in the Red River Valley. After helping one young man, Frank Feibirger, he remained as a hired 

hand on their farm for twelve years and later acquired a

6Ibid. ; Casselton Reporter, April 10, 1936; Fargo Forum, April 11, 1936. Many sources state that Frank Langer homesteaded; his daughters, however, recalled that he purchased 

his land. According to correspondence with Cass County Register of Deeds, A. Friedman, April 6, 1967, the earliest record of Frank Langer obtaining land was October 23, 1884, 

when he purchased the NW*s of Section 22 of Everest Township from William Nicolay. The records indicate he bought more 

land in the area during later years. There is, however, no record of land purchases by Frank Langer prior to 1884. 

7Casselton Reporter, September 26, 1941; interview 

with Mrs. Mary Ford (one of William Langer's sisters), Casselton, North Dakota, March 14, 1967. 4

farm of his own in the area.8 

In 1879 Frank Langer became active in community affairs by being one of the settlers who gathered to hold Mass and organize the parish of St. Leo. The parish was organized with the help of the Reverend Father Spitzenberger who rode horseback some twenty miles from Moorhead, Minnesota, to celebrate the Mass.^ 

Although he was involved with the founding of the parish and was a supporter of the Church, Frank Langer was not a strong, "church-going" Catholic. He was a Mason when he married, and the marriage ceremony was performed by ajustice of the peace. Even though the marriage was later blessed by the Church, he continued his membership in the lodge and eventually reached the thirty-second degree rank. During the last years of his life, however, he left the lodge, came back into the Church, and was later buried within the parish of St. Leo.1® 

In 1884 Langer started a general store in Everest and became both postmaster and town clerk.11 By 1889 he was a

NO STONE UNTURNED: LANGER AS STATES ATTORNEY 

In the months following his triumph at the polls the States Attorney-elect continued his work as Assistant States Attorney which would give an indication of what Morton County citizens could expect from him in the future. The initial move came when F. L. Watkins of the North Dakota Enforcement League filed a complaint with the States Attorney after charging that men in nearly every town across the southern part of the county were violating the prohibition laws. Because of the complaint, the States Attorney's office began actions to bring the lawbreakers to justice.*" 

Langer, however, led a raid on the prohibition violators, colloquially referred to as "blind piggers," in the town of Hebron in the northern part of the county. The raid was so successful that two railroad freight cars were used to bring the confiscated evidence of 4,850 gallons of mostly high-priced wines back to Mandan for use as evidence in connection with the warrants issued for the several “blind piggers" involved.* 2

CHAPTER IV

CONCLUSION 

Although he was a farmer's son, Langer quite early in his life developed the desire to enter the law profession He successfully completed Law School at the University of North Dakota before he was old enough to practice in the state. DemonsLraLiny continued eagerness, he furthered his education at Columbia University where he became one of the outstanding members of his class. 

Returning to North Dakota, Langer revealed his 

intense desires and political objectives when he disclosed: 

I desire now to make a living and a record so Imay one day become popular enough to be the most popular man in the state just like I was in college and be given some political office large enough to attract the notice of my former classmates in the East.2 

Beginning as Morton County Assistant States Attorney Langer displayed eagerness for advancement. When the opportunity came, he exhibited political skill by overcoming strong opposition, in winning his first political office as 

^-Interviews with Mrs. Woell ana Mrs. Ford, March 14, 1967, and Mrs. McGurren, March 2, 1967. Each of the sisters interviewed recalled that their brother did not dislike farming and farm work, but he never desired to become afarmer as the law profession was bis ambition. 

^William Langer to Mrs. Charles M. Rolker, Sr., May 18, 1911, Langer Papers, Box One, File Folder One, Personal File to 1914. 

> 8 8

States Attorney of Morton County. Daring his first year as 

States Attorney, he made himself known throughout the state as a conscientious, energetic, and colorful official. To 

many he was a model of everything that a public servant should be. 

Capitalizing on his flowering reputation and riding 

the political movement of the Nonpartisan League, Langer 

attained the attorney generalship of the state with an impressive victory in both the primary and general elections. 

Langer' s record as States Attorney became the key in his successful bid for the attorney generalship. Was this 

record the result of his desire to uphold the law, or was 

there another motive? Were the tasks undertaken by him as 

States Attorney originally his ideas, stemming from his regard 

for the law, or were they political expediencies as suggested 

by his friend, Dan Brennan? 

Certainly, Brennan's many suggestions cannot be discredited. Langer's course of action, following his correspondence with Brennan, was precisely what Brennan 

advised, and the eventual results were what he predicted. 

But, Langer had long before initiated his crackdown on prohibition violators in Morton County which brought his widest publicity. 

Judging from his own writing and his correspondence with Brennan and others, it is evident that Langer had high ambitions when he came to North Dakota and when he began his activities in Morton County. His desire to obtain high 

89 9 0 

office and make a name for himself explains his driving 

determination from the day he took office as States Attorney 

until he was confident of election as attorney general. 

Regardless of his motives, Langer's performance as a public 

servant was commendable and worthy of reward. 

According to the election returns, Langer was one 

of the most popular candidates on the ballot. Only the 

ticket leader Frazier and the incumbent Secretary of State, Thomas Hall, received more votes than Langer.^ With this 

victory Langer attaineu a substantial political office, but 

attorney generals of small midwestern states usually did not 

receive much publicity outside of their own states. 

Therefore, was this the office of his expressed 

desires, or was there still another step up the poltical 

ladder before he would feel that he had reached his ultimate 

ambitions? Would the attorney generalship bring him the 

kind of publicity that would make him the most popular 

man in the state and make him well known outside of the 

state? Based on his past behavior and actions, a logical 

conclusion would be that William Langer would soon make 

another attempt to move upward politically in North Dakota. 

Early in 1916, Langer's fellow Progressive, Usher 

L. Burdick, had mentioned in a letter, "It may be that we 

^Election Returns, 1916 General Election, Frazier received 87,665 votes, Hall 84,671, and Langer 79,783. 91 

shall have to run you for governor. . ."4 and long before 

this the Columbia University 1910 class prophecy had revealed 

. . . To Washington was my next excursion and I

hastened to the office of the third successful 

politician of our country who could at the same 

time be fearless and truthful. The first Lincoln, 

the second Roosevelt and the third Bill Langer. 

He held no position except his seat in the Senate, 

but his influence pervaded Washington as subtly 

as it at one time did our own campus. When I

entered the door to the inner sanctum I noticed 

above it was hung the old proverb, 'To The Victor 

Belongs the Spoils.' Optimistic Bill met me half 

way and he was the same old Bill always glad to 

have a fellow drop in on him no matter how busy 

he was.5 

Both Burdick and the Columbia prophecy proved cor 

rect. North Dakotans would in the future elect William 

Langer as their governor and later send him to Washington 

as their United States Senator. 

4Usher L. Burdick to William Langer, January 11, 

1916, Langer Papers, Box One, File Folder Twelve, Political 

File, January 1 to February 29, 1916. 

^Columbia Spectator, Columbia University, New York 

City, May 30 , 1910. This issue was located in the personal 

papers of Mrs. Gokey.

Ronald Vern Olson was born at Minot, North Dakota, on August 8, 1943. After attending a rural, elementary school, he attended Sherwood High School, Sherwood, North Dakota, and graduated in 1961. From 1961 to 1965, he attended Minot State College and received the Bachelor of Science Degree in June, 1965. During 1965-1966, he taught social studies at Des Lacs High School, Des Lacs, North Dakota. In June, 1966, he enrolled in the graduate school at the University of North Dakota at Grand Forks and in June, 1967, received the Master of Arts Degree in history. While at the University of North Dakota, he was a graduate teaching assistant in the Department of History and a member of Phi Alpha Theta, honorary history society. During the 

1967 summer session at the University of North Dakota, he will be a Visiting Lecturer in History. In the fall of

**Everest** is an [unincorporated community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unincorporated_area "Unincorporated area") in [Everest Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest_Township,_Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Everest Township, Cass County, North Dakota"), [Cass County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Cass County, North Dakota"), [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). It is located south of [Casselton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casselton,_North_Dakota "Casselton, North Dakota"), and was [platted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plat "Plat") in 1881. The post office was established in 1882 and operated until 1908. Everest was originally at the junction of the [Great Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_/(U.S./) "Great Northern Railway (U.S.)") and the [Northern Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway"), but the westernmost of the two rail lines was removed circa 1896 when it was acquired by the Great Northern Railway.

Everest was the birthplace of North Dakota governor (and later US senator) [William Langer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer "William Langer"), and the Langer family, including William's father Frank and uncle Joseph, were prominent residents of the Everest area during the late 1800s. Other noted residents were James Trammell, Edward Meilicke, Edward Redmon, Edward Weber, Edward Arnold, William MacFadden, and August Hilke, each of whom served as Everest Township or Cass County officials. Other prominent residents of Everest included Herbert Nilles, who was elected to the presidency of the North Dakota State Bar, and Morgan Ford, who was appointed as a judge to the US Customs Court.

Everest was the site of a railroad depot, a post office, two hotels, a school, a church, two general stores, two saloons, a butcher shop, a blacksmith shop, a lumber yard, four grain elevators, a harness maker, and other businesses. Everest once reported over 200 residents and was considered a prosperous community in the late 1800s. However, the removal of the rail line, closure of the post office, and a series of disastrous fires led to a decline in the community. By 1960, most of Everest's establishments had long since closed, leaving Everest with a population of 10 that year. Everest has been removed from official county maps.

Everest is 20 miles (32 km) from Fargo, the county seat.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-TAL-2) It is 2 miles (3.2 km) south of [Casselton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casselton,_North_Dakota "Casselton, North Dakota").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3) Everest lies at the junction of [North Dakota Highway 18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Highway_18 "North Dakota Highway 18") and 155th Avenue SE, near the [Casselton Robert Miller Regional Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casselton_Robert_Miller_Regional_Airport "Casselton Robert Miller Regional Airport").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CCND-township-4)

Everest is mostly located in section 15 of [Everest Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest_Township,_Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Everest Township, Cass County, North Dakota"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Polk-5) in southeastern North Dakota. The Durbin-Everest Channel, an intermittent stream, flows south of Everest, while the Wheatland Channel, another intermittent stream, runs north of Everest. Both streams are tributaries of Swan Creek.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-ARCGIS-6)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Everest%2C_North_Dakota%2C_plat_map_in_1893.png/250px-Everest%2C_North_Dakota%2C_plat_map_in_1893.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Everest,_North_Dakota,_plat_map_in_1893.png)

Everest, Dakota Territory, plat map in 1893

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Cass_County%2C_Dakota_Territory%2C_1886.png/250px-Cass_County%2C_Dakota_Territory%2C_1886.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cass_County,_Dakota_Territory,_1886.png)

Everest in Cass County, Dakota Territory, in 1886

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Ripon%2C_Buffalo%2C_Wheatland%2C_Sidney%2C_Casselton%2C_Everest%2C_Greene%2C_Mapleton%2C_Durbin%2C_Dalrymple%2C_North_Dakota_1895.png/250px-Ripon%2C_Buffalo%2C_Wheatland%2C_Sidney%2C_Casselton%2C_Everest%2C_Greene%2C_Mapleton%2C_Durbin%2C_Dalrymple%2C_North_Dakota_1895.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ripon,_Buffalo,_Wheatland,_Sidney,_Casselton,_Everest,_Greene,_Mapleton,_Durbin,_Dalrymple,_North_Dakota_1895.png)

Everest, in Dakota Territory, in 1895, showing the location of the community south of [Casselton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casselton,_North_Dakota "Casselton, North Dakota"), on the Durbin to Sidney rail line

Everest began as a railroad station on the [St. Paul, Minneapolis, and Manitoba Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Paul,_Minneapolis_and_Manitoba_Railway "Saint Paul, Minneapolis and Manitoba Railway") (also known as the Great Northern Railway).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-DOIS-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-MSBI-8) In August 1880, the Casselton Branch Railroad Company (CB) was incorporated by the [Northern Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway") (NP). Construction began on a railroad line joining the Northern Pacific's railroad in Cass County with a station in [Traill County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traill_County "Traill County").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-History-9)

Everest was [platted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plat "Plat") in 1881,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3) with the town divided into twelve blocks. The east–west streets were named A, B, C, and D Streets, with the north–south streets being named Front, Second, Third, and Fourth Streets. Manvell Street ran diagonally along the line of the Great Northern Railroad. The community was built directly west and south of the rail line.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-PBCCND-10) By the late 1880s, Everest was considered a "small town in Cass County \[...\] some 20 miles from [Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota "Fargo, North Dakota")."[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-DTSC-11)

There is some controversy surrounding the naming of the community. Some sources report that the community was named after the editor of _The [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon,_North_Dakota "Lisbon, North Dakota") Star_, but his name was Charles Everitt.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3)

During the summer of 1881, Everest was in development; the railroad line between [Casselton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casselton,_North_Dakota "Casselton, North Dakota") and Everest had not yet been completed, and a stagecoach line connected the two communities. The first hotel in Everest was a primitive affair, with one traveler, Mary E. Hogue Black, a schoolteacher in Casselton, reporting, "As there was not any R.R. track between Everest and Casselton, I had to go by stage to Everest, where I waited, with others, for the train which failed to come. Waiting all day and no train coming, we went to a so-called Hotel for the night, where I walked between two rows of men on the floor, heads to the walls and path at their feet, to reach my bed-room, separated by a lath partition from the men’s room, sharing my room with another woman, a stranger."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-12)

In October 1882, an agreement between the Northern Pacific and the Great Northern railroads transferred the Casselton Branch from the Northern Pacific to the Great Northern Railway. The Great Northern then began a project to connect the 3 miles (4.8 km) between its lines to the Casselton Branch terminus at Everest.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-History-9) The rail line connecting the two railroads was announced to be nearing completion in October 1882.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-BT1-13) After completion of the connection, Everest was at the junction of the Waupeton-Ripon railroad line (between [Durbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durbin,_North_Dakota "Durbin, North Dakota") and [Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sidney,_North_Dakota&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sidney, North Dakota (page does not exist)")) and the Casselton-Larimore rail line (at the terminus of that line).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-DOIS-7) The Everest post office was established on May 24, 1882; Carl Knoppel was the postmaster.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3)

On January 18, 1884, [Everest Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest_Township "Everest Township") was established. This township, along with [Walberg Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walberg_Township,_Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Walberg Township, Cass County, North Dakota"), were the first civil townships established in Cass County.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDM-14) By this time, Everest was the site of "two general stores, a butcher shop, a blacksmith shop, a lumber yard, and two hotels, one of which proudly advertised its fine horses. There was a post office and a one-room school."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Geelan-15) The postmaster in 1884 was J.H. Rodenberg.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-16)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Portrait_of_William_Langer%2C_circa_1919.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_William_Langer%2C_circa_1919.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_William_Langer,_circa_1919.jpg)

William Langer, circa 1919

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Joseph_Langer_1900.png/250px-Joseph_Langer_1900.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Langer_1900.png)

Joseph Langer in 1900

[William Langer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Langer "William Langer"), who later twice served as [governor of North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_North_Dakota "Governor of North Dakota"), was born in Everest in 1886 (he served as governor from 1933 to 1934, and from 1937 to 1939).[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Capace-17) William Langer's father, Frank, co-owned Everest's first general store and had also helped establish the community of Everest, as he was an investor in new towns.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Geelan-15) In addition to the general store, Frank Langer also became the postmaster in 1884, and in 1889, he was elected to the 11th district in the lower house of the newly created North Dakota state legislature; he served one term, and then returned to farming.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Olson-18) He later became a Cass County commissioner.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Geelan-15) The Langer family later moved to nearby Casselton, where William graduated from Casselton High School.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDGovernors-19)

William and Frank Langer were not the only notable Langers in Everest: Frank's brother Joseph (born January 22, 1852) moved to Dakota Territory with him and helped establish the community. Joseph claimed a [tree farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_farm "Tree farm") in Everest Township in 1877, and also invested in a mercantile in [Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope,_North_Dakota "Hope, North Dakota"). He was a member of the Masonic Lodge. He also served on the Everest Township board of supervisors for over a decade.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Compendium-20) The Langer family eventually owned many parcels of land surrounding Everest, Casselton, and other neighboring townships: according to Olsen (1967), "They owned eleven quarters in Everest \[Township\], three quarters in [Maple River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_River_Township,_Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Maple River Township, Cass County, North Dakota") \[Township\], two quarters in [Casselton Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casselton_Township,_Cass_County,_North_Dakota "Casselton Township, Cass County, North Dakota"), and much of the south half of section 35 in Casselton Township--the townsite section\[...\] The atlas also showed that Joseph Langer owned fourteen quarters of land in Casselton and Everest townships in 1906."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Olson-18)

Among the other prominent residents of the Everest area was Edward Meilicke, who farmed in Everest Township and who also operated a mercantile in the community. Meilicke settled in the area in 1882, and served for 15 years as the chairman of the Everest Township board of supervisors. Meilicke was later profiled in an early history of North Dakota.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Compendium-20)

Another prominent resident was August Hilke (born in Germany on November 18, 1837), who was among the earliest of the white settlers in Cass County. Hilke's family emigrated to Dodge County, Wisconsin in the United States in 1852; Hilke moved to Casselton in 1878, and from there settled in section 23 of Everest Township in 1880. His wife passed in 1884, and he married Cora Clark in 1885. He became a member of the Cass County board of supervisors, was the school treasurer, and joined the Odd Fellows and the Ancient Order of United Workmen. In 1900, according to one state history, he was "the fortunate possessor of one of the best farms of Cass County, and his residence on section 23, of Everest Township, is evidence of his prosperity and thrift."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-21)

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/James_D_Trammell_1900.png/250px-James_D_Trammell_1900.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_D_Trammell_1900.png)

James D Trammell in 1900

James D. Trammell was another prominent resident of Everest. Trammell was a transplant from [Fairfax County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") who settled in Everest in 1883. Trammell served on the Everest Township board of supervisors, and was also a member of the area's [Masonic Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masonic_Hall "Masonic Hall") and [Odd Fellows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Order_of_Odd_Fellows "Independent Order of Odd Fellows") fraternal order.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Compendium-20)

Other prominent men of Everest included Edward Redmon and William MacFadden. Edward Redmon was born in [Davenport, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenport,_Iowa "Davenport, Iowa") in 1856. He moved to the Everest area in 1877, when he went to North Dakota to claim land. He owned three sections of land, and also farmed in a fourth. He was a chairman of the Everest Township board of supervisors for many years. William McFadden was born in [Mount Vernon, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Vernon,_Ohio "Mount Vernon, Ohio") in 1857. He emigrated to Everest in 1885, where he became a grain buyer and farmer, purchasing land there. He was appointed deputy county treasurer, and later the cashier of the Cass County State Bank of Casselton. He was elected as Cass County treasurer in 1894 and was re-elected in 1896.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Compendium-20)

Edward Weber (born in [Landskron, Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Landskron,_Austria&action=edit&redlink=1 "Landskron, Austria (page does not exist)"), September 28, 1849) was another of the early residents of the Everest area. He came to the United States in 1867, marrying Rosa Stanger in 1871. He visited Cass County in 1877 with Frank and Joseph Langer. He settled in section 9 of Everest Township, where he bought land for himself, his brother, and his father circa 1877. By 1900, he owned five sections of land in the area. He served as an Everest Township official and also worked as a county assessor.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-22)

Circa 1888, Everest was the site of four [grain elevators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_elevator "Grain elevator"): the Cargill Elevator Company, the St. Anthony Elevator Company, the Northwestern Elevator Company, and the Mt. Vernon Elevator Company.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Executive-23) Everest was also the site of a branch of the Beidler and Robinson Lumber Company.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-24) The population of the community was estimated as 200 in 1890.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-LCA-25)

The Everest School was built in 1881. It was originally located in a field 0.5 miles (0.80 km) west of the main structures, which was hazardous during blizzards. A rope was strung between the village and the school to prevent schoolchildren from becoming lost during snowstorms. Eventually, the school was moved into the village.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-18-26) The Everest School District was originally numbered 102.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-SHSND-27) The Everest school building, a [one-room schoolhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-room_schoolhouse "One-room schoolhouse"),[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-WestFH-28) was just one of 182 schools in Cass County at that time. Two teachers were employed by the school during that era.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-29) The school building was also used as an official polling location.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-FFADR-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-FFADR2-31)

Two additional schools operated in the area: the Goshen School and the Langer School. These were small Everest Township schools.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-19-32)

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Everest%2C_North_Dakota_1886_fire.png/250px-Everest%2C_North_Dakota_1886_fire.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Everest,_North_Dakota_1886_fire.png)

Newspaper article announcing the 1886 Everest fire

[![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Everest%2C_Dakota_Territory%2C_1895_-_depot%2C_train%2C_and_elevator.png/250px-Everest%2C_Dakota_Territory%2C_1895_-_depot%2C_train%2C_and_elevator.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Everest,_Dakota_Territory,_1895_-_depot,_train,_and_elevator.png)

Everest, Dakota Territory, 1895, showing the railroad depot, a train, and a grain elevator

In November 1886, a fire destroyed part of Everest, including the business district.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-33) The fire made state headlines and destroyed Rodenberg and Langer's general store, two saloons, the hotel, McFadden and Siddell's hardware store, Wilson's boarding house, and the post office.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-34) The fire began in a vacant hotel room.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-WT-35)

The [Moravian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moravian_Church "Moravian Church") operated in Everest during this era. William Stengel led the congregation, circa 1887.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Moravian-36)

In 1888, severe frosts in the months of May, June, and August "knocked the wheat crop to the dogs" in the [Red River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Valley "Red River Valley"). The eastern half of the state was badly affected, and the following year, there was a terrible drought "such as was never known in Dakota", which destroyed the next round of crops. Area farmers suffered, and many were close to starvation. Frank Langer, one of the county commissioners, advocated for a [poor farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poor_farm "Poor farm") to be located in nearby Casselton, but was outvoted by the other Cass County commissioners, and the poor farm was instead built 3.5 miles (5.6 km) north of [Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota "Fargo, North Dakota").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Hoffbeck-37)

Everest had been founded in Cass County, in the northern half of Dakota Territory. When North Dakota and South Dakota were split and became states, they were both admitted on November 2, 1889.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-38) When the new state of North Dakota's first territorial legislature met, the state was divided into 31 congressional districts. The 11th Congressional District was a portion of Cass County: the townships of "Webster, Rush River, Hunter, Arthur, Amenia, Everest, Maple River, Leonard, Dows, Erie, Empire, Wheatland, Gill, Walburg, Watson, Page, Rich, Ayr, Buffalo, Howes, Eldrid, Highland, Rochester, Lake, Cornell, Tower, Hill, Clifton and Pontiac"; the district was entitled to one state senator and three state representatives. The state representatives included Everest resident Frank J Langer.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-39)

In March 1894, the business district of Everest was again wiped out by fire. The fire was estimated to have done $35,000 in damage (equivalent to $1,132,000 in 2024).[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-BWT2-40) At the time of the fire, the _Hope (North Dakota) Pioneer_ saltily reported, "The town of Everest, Cass county, was nearly wiped out of existence by fire early Sunday morning. Jim Hill's depot didn't burn, much to the regret of all the travelers along the line who have been compelled to wait upon trains within its dirty walls."[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-41)

Around that time, in either 1895 or 1896, the westernmost of the two railroad lines was pulled up, as the Great Northern Railroad Company's plans for expansion had changed.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-History-9) This was a 4.79 miles (7.71 km)-long rail line connecting the towns of Everest and [Fleming](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fleming,_North_Dakota&action=edit&redlink=1 "Fleming, North Dakota (page does not exist)").[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-42) This was done because the Great Northern Railway was operating two parallel branch rail lines; it was stated that "for the sake of greater efficiency and the economy attained through elimination of unneeded trackage", the line between Fleming and Everest was no longer needed.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-43) The removal of the rail line would, in retrospect, cause a decline for Everest.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-18-26)

At this time, Everest was still considered a prosperous community, with one author writing in 1895, "The thriving towns of Everest, Casselton, and [Amenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenia,_North_Dakota "Amenia, North Dakota") are seen in their order from south to north; and at these and many smaller stations of both the Northern Pacific and Great Northern Railways, also on some of the large farms, \[grain\] elevators tower above the flat lands, waiting to be filled with their grain. It is a most beautiful prospect, completely characteristic of the Red River Valley."[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Upham-44)

### Early twentieth century

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Everest,_North_Dakota&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early twentieth century")\]

[![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Everest%2C_North_Dakota%2C_in_1906.png/250px-Everest%2C_North_Dakota%2C_in_1906.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Everest,_North_Dakota,_in_1906.png)

Everest, North Dakota, in 1906, showing the removed railroad line

In 1900, a loading station on the Northern Pacific Railway was named Langers, after both Joseph and Frank Langer.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Williams-45) This station was just northeast of Everest.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Topoview-46)

The population of Everest was 213 in 1900.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CMA-47) Circa 1906, Everest was the site of three grain elevators: those of the St. Anthony and Dakota Elevator Company, the Cargill Elevator Company, and the Northwestern Elevator Company.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPSC-48) Everest received mail daily, had telephone service, and was the site of a harness maker and a blacksmith shop. Stagecoaches ran daily between Everest and Casselton.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Gazetteer-49)

The railroad depot in Everest closed in July 1903, and at that time there were reports that the post office would close as well.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-50) In 1903, Henry Albright succeeded James B. Coyle as the Everest postmaster.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-51) Paul Schiebold was the postmaster circa 1906.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Gazetteer-49) The Everest post office closed in 1908.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-PH-52) Mail was subsequently routed through nearby Casselton.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3)

By this time, several members of the Langer family had left Everest, and a new generation of businessmen operated in the community. Among these was Edward Arnold. Arnold, born in [Lockport, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockport,_New_York "Lockport, New York") on March 18, 1874, relocated to Everest and was involved in the grain business by around 1914. He became the manager of the Northwestern Elevator Company in Everest, and became a well-known resident of the community. He was a member of the [Ancient Order of United Workmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Order_of_United_Workmen "Ancient Order of United Workmen") (AOUW) and the [Brotherhood of American Yeomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brotherhood_of_American_Yeomen "Brotherhood of American Yeomen") (BAY).[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-53)

Another prominent resident was Herbert G Nilles, who was born in Everest in 1894. While in law school be was member of the [Phi Delta Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Delta_Phi "Phi Delta Phi") legal fraternity. He was admitted to the North Dakota Bar in 1917. In 1932, he was elected to membership in the North Dakota Chapter of the [Order of the Coif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Coif "Order of the Coif").[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Burdick-54)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-55) He relocated to Fargo and was elected president of the State Bar Association of North Dakota in 1939.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-56)

[![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Morgan_J_Ford_Cass_County_ND.png/250px-Morgan_J_Ford_Cass_County_ND.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Morgan_J_Ford_Cass_County_ND.png)

Morgan J. Ford, in 1906

Another prominent resident was Morgan Ford, who was born on a farm near [Wheatland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheatland,_North_Dakota "Wheatland, North Dakota") on September 8, 1911. Ford was the son of Morgan J Ford and Mary Langer Ford. After graduating from Casselton High School and the [University of North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Dakota "University of North Dakota"), Ford returned to Cass County and taught at the Everest School for one year (1934-1935). He became the Casselton city attorney in 1942, and was nominated by [President Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Harry_S._Truman "President Harry S. Truman") to be a judge of the [United States Customs Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Customs_Court "United States Customs Court") in 1949.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-57)

[![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Everest_and_Casselton%2C_ND_area%2C_1920.png/250px-Everest_and_Casselton%2C_ND_area%2C_1920.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Everest_and_Casselton,_ND_area,_1920.png)

Everest and surrounding communities in 1920

In 1920, the population of Everest was 64.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-PAW-58) In 1922, there was again a fire in Everest. This fire destroyed the Northwestern Elevator Company's building in Everest, and according to a news report in the _[Jamestown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown,_North_Dakota "Jamestown, North Dakota") Weekly Alert_, "had the breeze prevailed toward the stores southeast of the elevator little would have been left of the town, as it was only hard work that saved the depot." According to that report, around 6,000 bushels of wheat were in the elevator at the time of the fire. The cause of the fire was unknown, with one theory being that the fire was caused by sparks from the nearby railroad, or due to friction.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-59)

In 1923, the Everest School District covered 13.5 square miles (35 km2). At that time, Cass County had 142 operating schools. The Everest School District had by this point been renumbered 90.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-60) In 1928, a basement was added below the Everest Schoolhouse.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-18-26) In 1939, the Langer School closed, due to low enrollment.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-19-32)

During William Langer's gubernatorial race of 1936, it was reported that 100% of the residents of Everest Township voted for him. Similarly, it was claimed that all voters of Everest Township (63 residents) endorsed him during his Senate race of 1952.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-BT-61)

[![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Everest%2C_North_Dakota.jpg/250px-Everest%2C_North_Dakota.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Everest,_North_Dakota.jpg)

Everest in 2009

The population of Everest was estimated at 100 in 1940; the other communities along the former rail line were smaller, with [Durbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durbin,_North_Dakota "Durbin, North Dakota") reporting 22 residents and Fleming reporting 10 residents.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-TAL-2) During that era, Everest still appeared on North Dakota state maps.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-ND1930-62)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-63) The general store in Everest closed in 1942.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-18-26)

In September 1949, enrollment at the Everest School was 17 students.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CCR-64)

### Late twentieth century

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Everest,_North_Dakota&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Late twentieth century")\]

In 1952, William Langer, by that point a [U.S. Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), attempted to legally reclaim 2 acres (8,100 m2) of land in the Everest area, which had been deeded to the county back in 1911 by his father, Frank Langer. Langer stated that the contract stipulated that the land would be improved, with a road and a bridge across a [coulee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coulee "Coulee"). He stated that no bridge or road had been constructed, and he thus requested that the land be returned to the Langers.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-BT3-65) Langer passed on November 8, 1959.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NGA-66)

In 1960, [Interstate 94](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94 "Interstate 94") replaced State Highway 10 between Casselton and Everest, on the northern edge of Everest Township.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-19-32)

By 1960, the population of Everest had dropped to 10.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3) In 1962, the Everest School District #90 reported zero students.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Census1960-67) That year, both the Everest School and the Goshen School closed, consolidated into the Casselton School District.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-19-32) In 1968, the Casselton Elevator Company and feed plant burned to the ground; it was not rebuilt.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-19-32)

By 1975, Agnes Geelan wrote that Everest was just "a memory, its chief claim to fame being that 'Bill Langer was born on a farm near Everest'."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-Geelan-15) In 1979, it was reported that just four families lived in Everest, and no businesses remained in the community.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CND1979-18-26)

Douglas Wick (1988) writes, "the village existed for many years," but the closure of the railroad station and post office, along with the removal of one of the rail lines, and a disastrous fire, helped lead to its eventual decline.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-NDPN-3) Frank Weber, a longtime resident of Everest (beginning in 1893), blamed the automobile for the decline of Everest, stating, "Everest was a nice little town. That was our home trading post when we farmed on our home place, but as soon as the automobile came the people then left Everest and went on to Casselton because there was more stores, and of course more selection of good and all this and that. And then all these little towns lost out, including Everest."[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-68)

Today, Everest is in the Central Cass Public School District.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-SA-69) Everest no longer appears on official county maps.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CCND2-70)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CCND3-71) The population of all of [Everest Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest_Township "Everest Township") in 2020 was just 36 residents, with 8 households.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest,_North_Dakota#cite_note-72)

"County (United States)") in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota"). As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the population was 184,525,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-2020_Census_\(City\)-1) making it the [most populous county in North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_counties_in_North_Dakota "List of counties in North Dakota"), and was estimated to be 200,945 in 2024, almost twice the population of [Burleigh County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burleigh_County,_North_Dakota "Burleigh County, North Dakota"), the second most populated county in the state.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-QF-2) It contains over 25.23% of the state's population.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-3) The [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") is [Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo,_North_Dakota "Fargo, North Dakota"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-4) the state's [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_North_Dakota "List of cities in North Dakota"). The county is named for [George Washington Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Cass "George Washington Cass"), president of the [Northern Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway") from 1872 to 1875. It is the only Cass County in the United States that is not named after [Lewis Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Cass "Lewis Cass"). Cass County is part of the [Fargo, ND-Moorhead, MN Metropolitan Statistical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo%E2%80%93Moorhead "Fargo–Moorhead"). Cass County was defined by action of the [Dakota Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_Territory "Dakota Territory") legislature on January 4, 1873, and its organization was affected on October 27 of that year. It was named for railroad executive [George Washington Cass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Cass "George Washington Cass") (1810–1888).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-5) Its boundaries were altered in 1875, and in 1961.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-7) Cass County lies on the east side of North Dakota. Its east boundary line abuts the west boundary line of the state of [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") across the river. The [Red River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North") flows northward along the county's east boundary, on its way to Lake Winnipeg and Hudson Bay. The county's terrain consists of low rolling hills, devoted to agriculture except around developed areas.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-CCND-8) Its terrain slopes to the north and east, with its highest point on the southwestern corner at 1,194 ft (364 m) ASL.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-9) According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the county has a total area of 1,767.811 square miles (4,578.61 km2), of which 1,764.935 square miles (4,571.16 km2) is land and 2.876 square miles (7.45 km2) (0.16%) is water.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-10) It is the 10th largest county in North Dakota by total area.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_County,_North_Dakota#cite_note-11) * [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") _[Empire Builder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_Builder "Empire Builder")_ (_[Fargo station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo_station "Fargo station")_) * [Jefferson Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Lines "Jefferson Lines") * [MATBUS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MATBUS_/(Fargo-Moorhead/) "MATBUS (Fargo-Moorhead)") * [Traill County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traill_County,_North_Dakota "Traill County, North Dakota") - Jahner. Jahner has served as Sheriff of Cass County since January 2, 2019. The voters of Cass County have historically tended to vote Republican. As recently as the 2004 presidential election, [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") carried Cass County with nearly 60 percent of the vote. However, in recent elections, the county has become more politically diverse and competitive, particularly in Fargo. In 2008, Democratic candidate [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") won the majority of votes in Cass County, with a voting percentage very close to the percentage Obama received in the entire nation, while [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") won the majority of votes in North Dakota. [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney")'s winning margin in 2012 over Obama in Cass County was 49.9% to 47%, while [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") received 49.3% of votes in 2016 (52.69% in 2024), compared to 38.8% for [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") and 11.9% for third-party candidates. In 2018, Democratic Senator [Heidi Heitkamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidi_Heitkamp "Heidi Heitkamp") achieved a 14-point lead in Eastern North Dakota, although the state as a whole soundly elected Republican [Kevin Cramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Cramer "Kevin Cramer").
